content.title: About
content.content: Chicken with mole sauce is a classic Mexican dish where tender pieces of chicken are coated in a thick, aromatic sauce made from chilies, chocolate, nuts, and spices. The mole sauce balances heat, sweetness, and a hint of bitterness, creating a complex flavor profile.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: There are more than 20 varieties of mole, each differing in ingredients and level of spiciness.
Traditional mole is simmered for several hours, sometimes even days, to develop its depth of flavor.
Original recipes can contain over 30 ingredients, including dried fruits, spices, seeds, and even flowers.
Mole was considered the “sauce of the gods” in ancient Mexican cultures and is often served on special celebrations.
Chicken mole is commonly served with rice, corn tortillas, or beans.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Antioxidants from chocolate and spices
items.content: Cocoa and spices such as cinnamon and clove contain polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both chicken and some mole ingredients (e.g., nuts) supply B6 and B12 vitamins, important for nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Nuts and seeds add magnesium, iron, and zinc, supporting metabolism and immune function.

items.title: Low carbohydrate content
items.content: The dish fits moderate low‑carb diets because most carbs come from the sauce, not the protein.

items.title: Spiciness and spices
items.content: Mole can be very hot; individuals with sensitive stomachs should reduce the amount of chili.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: Recipes often include peanuts, almonds, or other nuts, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared mole can be salty; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of nuts and chocolate, the dish is relatively calorie‑rich, so watch serving sizes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the chicken hot, generously drizzled with mole sauce. It pairs well with steamed rice, quinoa, corn tortillas, or a fresh salad. A squeeze of lime adds a bright acidity.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. The sauce can be frozen separately in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese, meat and dark‑green vegetables, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of eggs cooked without added fat, combined with cheese, lean meat (such as ham or turkey) and dark‑green vegetables (spinach, broccoli, kale). Eggs provide high‑quality protein, while the vegetables add vitamins, minerals and dietary fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most nutrient‑dense foods, containing all essential amino acids.
Dark‑green vegetables are rich in chlorophyll, which may support natural detoxification processes.
A modest amount of cheese enhances calcium absorption from the eggs.
Cooking without added fat preserves the natural taste of the ingredients and reduces calorie count.
The meal can be prepared in a microwave or a steamer, retaining more nutrients.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: One large egg supplies about 6 g of protein, supporting muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin B12, riboflavin and folate, important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Source of vitamin D and selenium
items.content: The yolk is one of the few food sources of vitamin D and also provides selenium, an antioxidant mineral.

items.title: Dark‑green vegetables provide vitamin K and folate
items.content: Spinach and broccoli are high in vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Low in added fats
items.content: Absence of added oil reduces overall calories and saturated fat intake.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may develop an allergic reaction to egg proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: The yolk contains cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should moderate egg consumption.

items.title: Sodium in cheese and meat
items.content: Choose low‑salt cheese and lean, minimally processed meat to avoid excess sodium.

items.title: Oxalates in dark‑green vegetables
items.content: Large amounts of spinach can increase the risk of kidney stones in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Beat the eggs, stir in grated cheese, cooked lean meat and pre‑cooked or steamed dark‑green vegetables. Cook on a dry non‑stick pan or in a steamer, stirring until the mixture sets. Garnish with fresh herbs if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Keep raw ingredients separately: eggs in the fridge at +4 °C, cheese in the dairy compartment, meat in its original packaging for no more than 3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Graham crackers are whole‑grain dry biscuits made from whole wheat, barley and rye. In sandwich form they consist of two crackers with a sweet or creamy filling (such as jam, chocolate spread, or nut butter) placed between them.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Graham crackers were created in the United States in the late 19th century as a healthier alternative to sugary biscuits.
The traditional recipe uses cracked wheat flakes, giving the cracker a characteristic crunch and mild bitterness.
Sandwich versions appeared in the 1930s when manufacturers began adding sweet fillings for children.
Graham crackers are a key ingredient in the American dessert “crackerdough pudding.”
In Russia similar products are sold as “sandwich biscuits with filling.”

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole grains in the crackers provide fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Graham crackers release energy slowly, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, niacin and folate are present, contributing to normal metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many sweet cookies, Graham crackers contain relatively little fat.

items.title: Filling can boost protein
items.content: Using nut butter or cottage‑cheese spread as the filling adds protein to the snack.

items.title: Wheat/gluten allergy
items.content: Graham crackers contain gluten and are unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar in the filling
items.content: Sweet fillings may be high in sugar, which is a concern for diabetics or those watching their weight.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Consuming large amounts can cause a rapid rise in blood glucose.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Some brands add preservatives or artificial flavors.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Graham cracker sandwiches are a convenient snack, suitable for kids’ lunches or as a dessert. They pair well with milk, tea, or can be used as a base for cheesecake‑style desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in an airtight package. For longer shelf life keep refrigerated to prevent the filling from becoming stale.

content.title: About
content.content: Plain microwave popcorn is a ready‑to‑cook snack that expands in a microwave oven. The bag contains dried corn kernels that pop quickly when heated, forming light, airy pieces. The flavor is neutral, without added salt or seasonings, making it a versatile base for further topping.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn is one of the few corn varieties whose kernels “explode” due to high internal moisture when heated.
The first commercial microwave popcorn appeared in the United States in the 1980s.
Plain microwave popcorn is relatively low‑calorie: about 350 kcal per 100 g of popped product.
Unlike traditional stovetop popcorn, microwave bags often contain a small amount of oil and stabilizers to ensure even popping.

items.title: Low in added fat
items.content: Plain microwave popcorn contains little to no added oil, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Corn kernels are rich in dietary fiber, which supports digestive health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Popcorn provides polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Quick source of glucose
items.content: The carbohydrates in popcorn are rapidly digestible, offering a fast energy boost.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Corn is naturally gluten‑free, so popcorn is safe for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to corn, experiencing skin or gastrointestinal reactions.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Popcorn can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Burn hazard
items.content: Steam inside the bag becomes very hot; open it carefully to avoid burns.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Certain brands add preservatives or flavor enhancers; choose a product with minimal additives if you have a sensitive stomach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place the bag in the microwave, unfolding it according to the instructions. Cook on high power for 2–3 minutes, stopping when the interval between pops exceeds 2 seconds. Let the bag stand for a minute, then open, stir gently, and optionally season with salt, herbs, or cheese powder.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened bag in a cool, dry place away from moisture. After opening, transfer remaining kernels to an airtight container to maintain their popping ability.

pork-chow-mein-or-chop-suey-with-noodles.title: Pork Chow Mein or Chop Suey with Noodles

content.title: About
content.content: Pork Chow Mein and Chop Suey with noodles are popular Asian dishes featuring thinly sliced pork stir‑fried with vegetables and egg noodles. The quick, high‑heat cooking preserves the crispness of the veggies and the savory notes of soy sauce, ginger, and garlic.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chow Mein originated in Chinese cuisine but became widely known in the United States in the mid‑20th century.
Chop Suey is a “catch‑all” dish that uses whatever leftovers are on hand, making each recipe unique.
Traditional Chow Mein uses egg noodles, but rice or wheat noodles are also common variations.
Pork is often marinated in soy sauce, rice vinegar, and cornstarch to stay tender during stir‑fry.
The dishes are frequently finished with lime, fresh cilantro, and chili for extra brightness.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Pork provides a complete source of animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish supplies thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Pork and the mixed vegetables contribute iron, zinc, and selenium, important for immune function.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: Broccoli, carrots, bell peppers, and other veggies add dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: When prepared with minimal sweet sauces, the meal contains little added sugar, making it suitable for moderate carbohydrate diets.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and pre‑made seasoning blends can be salty; opt for low‑sodium soy sauce or use less.

items.title: Fat content of pork
items.content: Some cuts are fatty; choose lean cuts or trim excess fat before cooking.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: People allergic to soy should substitute soy sauce with tamari or coconut aminos.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Over‑cooking noodles at very high heat can produce acrylamide; stir‑fry quickly without burning.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, straight from the wok. Squeeze fresh lime, sprinkle cilantro, chili flakes, or crushed peanuts for extra texture. It pairs well with steamed rice or a simple cucumber salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers in an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in a skillet or microwave, adding a splash of water to restore noodle moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: Sushi with egg is a traditional Japanese dish consisting of vinegared rice wrapped in nori and topped with a thin layer of tamago (Japanese omelette). The egg adds a delicate flavor, slight sweetness, and extra protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tamago is often seasoned with soy sauce, sugar, and mirin, giving it a characteristic golden hue.
Egg sushi is commonly served as a cucumber roll (kappa maki) with cucumber inside as well.
In Japan, egg symbolizes prosperity and is frequently served during celebrations.
Tamago sushi is often used as a filler between more expensive ingredients in sushi bars.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs provide a complete source of high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Tamago supplies vitamin B12, riboflavin, and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Eggs contain iron, phosphorus, and selenium, important for blood health and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Egg sushi fits moderate low‑carb diets, as the main carb source is rice while the egg adds minimal sugar.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in the yolk help maintain healthy vision.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolk contains cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should monitor portion size.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Improperly cooked egg can carry a risk of salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Egg sushi is usually eaten with chopsticks, sometimes lightly dipped in soy sauce. It pairs well with pickled ginger, wasabi, and marinated ginger.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared sushi in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for no more than 24 hours. For longer storage, keep the rice and egg separate to prevent the nori from becoming soggy.
